merged.title: fix(hostgen): hook points keep their tail call's result
merged.author: Drustburn
merged.untrustedBody:
## Summary

hostgen's `inherit_results` (cdb6d523) gives a definition matched as
returning nothing, whose last statement is a call, that call's result
type: the game's callers read the result register it leaves
(`void f(p) { g(p, 0x20); }` called as `int f(...)`). It leaves out the
functions the port wraps with host C of its own, by testing
`program.wrap`. Since 26e2d101 that set also holds every `hook` row
(hook points are kept as `<name>__game` too), and since the behaviour
catalogue's update functions became hook points (c027aecf), 13 of them
in rac1/pal no longer pass their tail call's result on, and with them
two wrappers that pass one of theirs on. The report's
`results_inherited` went from 166 to 151.

The one whose result the game reads is func_L00_00237B70
(Moby_Class482_Update): a name the catalogue folds over 105 places of
one shape (a jump to the place's own callee), among them the colour
tween of the particle code, `int (from, to, fraction)`.

| | Commit | Touches |
|---|-

opened.title: fix(port): the library layer answers as the console's libraries and kernel do
opened.author: Drustburn
opened.untrustedBody:
## Summary

The port answers the game's calls into Sony's libraries and the EE
kernel with host C of its own (`port/game/common/lib/*`, bound by each
game's `libraries.tsv`). A differential test against calls recorded
from the retail game in an emulator found places where those answers
differ from what the console's libraries and kernel give: return values
the kernel never returns, state kept in the port's statics where the
library keeps it in the game's memory, a guard that consulted a table
the console does not have, packets in the wrong layout, and library
functions answered by the port that only keep the game's own state and
can run the game's C. This PR fixes them.

Most of them change nothing a player sees in rac1 today (no caller
reads the value, or both sides happen to agree in a normal run); they
make the library layer's answers and the game's memory match the
console's, which is what the game's own code relies on. Where a commit
has a game-visible effect it says so.

opened.title: feat(port): the EE's float arithmetic for chosen functions, and port overrides of matched C
opened.author: Drustburn
opened.untrustedBody:
## Summary

Two pieces of infrastructure the port's remaining fixes build on, each
with one small real use as proof.

**1. The EE FPU's float arithmetic for C (`openrac/ps2float.h`,
hostgen.json `"ps2_float"`).** The port computes the game's floats in the
host's arithmetic, with the game's thread rounding toward zero and
denormals as zero (`openrac_ee_float_mode`) and `openrac_fdiv`'s
saturating divide. That is the EE's arithmetic for most of what the game
computes, but not all of it: the EE's adder drops the smaller operand's
bits more than one place below the larger one's last bit before it adds
(`1 - 1.5 * 2^-24` is `0x3F7FFFFF` on the console, `0x3F7FFFFE` on a host
rounding toward zero), a result past the largest float is `±0x7FFFFFFF`
(an infinity or FLT_MAX on the host), and an exponent of 255 is an
ordinary number. Where the game cuts a result to an integer, or compares
it, one last place decides. `port/assets/ps2_float.h` already models the
console's arithmetic on bit patterns

This follows #109. Two more level functions are assembly in the original. They are classified the way `docs/ASM_CLASSIFICATION.md` does it for level code: listed by hand in `config/overlays/handwritten_asm.txt`, their `INCLUDE_ASM` stubs become `ASM_FUNC`, and the report counts them as finished original-source work. `ASM_FUNC` is `INCLUDE_ASM`, so the same `asm/overlays/*.s` is included and the image does not change.

This needs no new rule. Each function is the level programs' copy of an executable function that `config/handwritten_asm.txt` already lists, so it uses the existing "listed by hand" rule (func_L00_00251328, func_L00_00251358, func_L00_002001D8).

## What

Two large level-20 (yeedil) bodies, transcribed almost completely and measured
thoroughly, with the compiler knowledge the work produced.

| function | size | level | state |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| `func_L11_0042F018` | 10,312 | 11 (joba) | 97% of the instructions match; 292 bytes short |
| `func_L04_002E7C08` | 14,304 | 4 (barlow) | the 80-byte prologue matches instruction for instruction; 272 bytes short |

measurement. The build is unaffected; `tools/build.py all` still prints 28 programs OK.

What the passes did settle is how a body of this size is built, and that is general:

- **The frame size is a formula, not a choice.** GCC 1.x lays it out as

opened.title: feat(src): two yeedil bodies freed by the grouped-copy profiles
opened.author: ReaperOfVeriod
opened.untrustedBody:
## What

Two level-20 (yeedil) bodies that the compiler's grouped-copy profiles free.

| function | size | residues before | now |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| `func_L20_0039C448` | 248 | the 128-bit copy, the order of the two saves | exact |
| `func_L20_0043D470` | 100 | the 128-bit copy, the float register order | exact |

Both are the records' own C, unchanged. The records' analysis of the wall
itself is kept in `docs/COMPILER-NOTES.md`.

## The wall, and what removes it

Of the 3,978 functions that live in level 20, **359** have the retail's shape for a
128-bit copy - an `addiu` whose destination is the base of a zero-displacement
`lq`/`sq` - and every one of them was behind the same fold: this cc1 folded the
constant offset back into the copy (`lq $v0,0x60($a1)` where the retail has
`addiu $a2,$a1,0x60 ; lq $v0,0x0($a2)`).

The mechanism was read out of the compiler's own source: the front end builds the
address as the pointer's pseudo, the CSE's `find_best_addr` (gcc/cse.c) subst
